headline_marked: [[PyTorch 2.13 FlexAttention]] on M1 Max is up to 7.83x faster for sparse attention
headline: PyTorch 2.13 FlexAttention on M1 Max is up to 7.83x faster for sparse attention
summary: New benchmarks show FlexAttention on Apple Silicon can significantly speed up AI model attention mechanisms for sparse data, though standard attention remains faster for dense patterns.
details: A new benchmark reveals that PyTorch 2.13's FlexAttention, when run on an M1 Max chip, can achieve up to a 7.83x speedup for sparse attention tasks. This optimization is crucial as attention mechanisms in AI models become computationally expensive with longer text inputs.

The experiment compared FlexAttention with standard Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA) on an M1 Max using 32,768 tokens and a 256-token local window. FlexAttention completed the task in 75.27 ms, compared to SDPA's 589.05 ms. However, for ordinary causal attention, SDPA was found to be approximately 19x faster.

FlexAttention, first announced as a prototype in October 2024, allows developers to define attention rules as Python functions. PyTorch's `torch.compile` then optimizes these into specialized fused kernels, enabling the skipping of unnecessary token comparisons.

The PyTorch 2.13 update, released on July 8, 2026, includes Metal/MPS kernels for FlexAttention on Apple Silicon, with PyTorch reporting potential performance gains of up to 12x for sparse patterns. However, the API and kernel options are still considered unstable.

The benchmark focused solely on the forward pass, excluding mask creation and compilation time. While FlexAttention showed significant speedups for sparse attention, its setup cost, including BlockMask construction and the initial compiled call, needs to be considered. For the tested 32,768 token scenario, the setup cost was recovered in about three forward passes.

headline_marked: [[Autonomous AI agents]] need a one-page contract to prevent errors
headline: Autonomous AI agents need a one-page contract to prevent errors
summary: A simple, one-page charter can define an AI agent's goals, powers, and guardrails, preventing common operational failures.
details: Running autonomous AI agents requires a management layer to ensure they operate effectively and safely. A one-page contract, or charter, serves as a crucial document that defines the agent's purpose, capabilities, and limitations.

The contract begins with a single-sentence goal, ensuring the agent can be optimized and audited. Vague objectives like 'grow the blog' are replaced with specific, measurable targets, such as 'Publish 1 search-optimized post daily; >100 search impressions by Aug 31'.

Autonomous powers are listed explicitly, defining what the agent is permitted to do. This prevents both timid agents that constantly seek permission and overly creative ones that invent their own permissions. Anything not listed is explicitly forbidden.

A critical 'guardrail' is the facts-only rule, requiring every reported number to have a live source or an honest 'unverified' tag. This transforms unreliable dashboards into trustworthy sources of actionable information.

Human-only blockers are also included to halt operations when critical issues arise, such as expired logins or missing API keys. This ensures these show-stopping problems receive immediate attention instead of being bypassed by the agent.
The report format is streamlined to five lines of facts only, ensuring readability. This prevents the common issue of long, unread reports that render the reporting mechanism useless.

Implementing this charter has revealed silent failures that previously went unnoticed, such as schedulers reporting success while publishing nothing, or dedup filters swallowing all items. These issues were previously masked by less rigorous reporting.
The author provides the charter template and two watchdog agents (ops-monitor, qa-reviewer) under an MIT license. A more comprehensive 'AI Employee Company Starter Kit' is also available.
